name: Orthodontic relapse retainer wear

card.summary: Wearing retainers after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their corrected positions, so the straight smile and tooth alignment people paid for stays in place.
card.note: Fixed retainers can trap plaque if not cleaned; retention plans are set by the treating orthodontist.

quick.overview:
Orthodontic relapse retainer wear is the practice of keeping teeth in the positions achieved by braces or clear aligners by wearing a retainer afterwards, often called retainer maxxing in online circles. The appearance payoff is that straight, evenly spaced front teeth stay that way instead of drifting back toward their old crowding.

Orthodontic references describe relapse as a lifelong possibility because the fibres and bone around teeth need time to adapt and because the mouth keeps changing with age. Studies comparing retainer types have generally found fixed lower retainers hold alignment best, with vacuum-formed clear retainers outperforming some other removable designs.
quick.how: Most people use a clear vacuum-formed retainer, a wire-and-acrylic Hawley retainer, or a thin wire bonded behind the front teeth. Removable types are usually worn overnight and taken out for eating, while bonded wires stay in place and are cleaned as part of the nightly routine. How long to wear them is decided by the orthodontist and can be a set period or indefinitely.
quick.risks: Removable retainers can be lost, can warp with heat and may wear through in people who grind their teeth. Bonded wires are harder to clean, which can lead to plaque build-up and gum inflammation. Wire breakage or detachment can allow teeth to move, so check-ups are part of retention.

lead: Orthodontic relapse retainer wear is the post-treatment practice of wearing retainers to keep teeth aligned after braces or aligners, a habit sometimes called retainer maxxing in looksmaxxing communities. It helps appearance by preserving the straight, evenly spaced smile that orthodontic treatment created, so the investment in alignment is not undone by teeth gradually shifting.[1]

Retainers are custom-made devices. Removable versions include the Hawley retainer, a wire across the front teeth attached to an acrylic palate plate, and the clear vacuum-formed retainer, a nearly invisible plastic shell. Fixed retainers are wires bonded to the back of the front teeth.[1] Retention is regarded in orthodontics as a long-term matter, with clinicians advising wear for a set period or indefinitely.[1]

Research on retention compares retainer types and asks how much late tooth movement is relapse versus normal ageing change. A 12-year follow-up of 92 treated patients tracked lower incisors in people with no retainer, a canine-to-canine bonded wire, or a wire bonded to all lower front teeth.[2][3] A 2023 study of 70 subjects compared Hawley and vacuum-formed upper retainers, each combined with a bonded lower retainer.[4]

chain: Retainer holds teeth in corrected positions
angle.text: A retainer keeps the tooth alignment gained from orthodontics visible in the smile over the years. People wear removable retainers at night or keep a bonded wire behind the front teeth so crowding and gaps do not return.

infobox: Removable: often overnight; duration set by orthodontist

paras: Retainers hold teeth while the periodontal fibres and surrounding bone adapt to their new positions. Orthodontic sources list several contributors to relapse: recoil of stretched gum and ligament fibres, pressure from lips, cheeks and tongue, the bite, and continued growth and ageing.[1]

Hawley retainers are among the oldest removable designs and can be adjusted but are more visible and can affect speech. Vacuum-formed retainers are favoured for appearance and lower cost but can wear out in people who grind their teeth. Fixed retainers need less patient cooperation but are harder to clean.[1]

In appearance-focused communities, retainer wear is treated as the maintenance step that protects the results of braces or aligners, since crowding of the lower front teeth is one of the most visible forms of relapse. Many participants describe continuing nightly wear for years after treatment, in line with what orthodontists commonly advise.

A European Journal of Orthodontics study followed 92 patients 12 years after treatment: 38 had no lower retainer, 24 had a spring hard wire bonded to the lower canines only, and 30 had a flexible wire bonded to all lower incisors and canines. Models taken before treatment, after treatment, and at 6 and 12 years were used to measure irregularity and canine width, and the authors aimed to separate relapse from natural growth changes.[2][3]

A Folia Medica study of 70 subjects compared maxillary Hawley or vacuum-formed retainers, each with a bonded mandibular retainer, assessing arch dimensions and tooth alignment during retention.[4] Review findings summarised on Wikipedia state that fixed retainers gave the best retention overall and vacuum-formed retainers held lower incisors better than other removable types.[1]
Fixed wires can accumulate plaque and contribute to gum inflammation if not cleaned well, and removable retainers should be kept clean and away from heat.[1]
